etymology: From Old English gerecenian, to recount or relate, cognate with German rechnen, to count. Webster 1828: to count, to compute, to esteem, to account. In the Authorized Version it is the accounting word of Romans 4, and it carries the whole doctrine of imputed righteousness on its back.
biblical_def: Reckoned is a ledger word, and the Holy Ghost chose a ledger word on purpose. Paul argues justification in Romans 4 out of the difference between wages and a gift: Now to him that worketh is the reward not reckoned of grace, but of debt (Romans 4:4). A wage is reckoned as debt, because it is owed. What God does with Abraham is entered on the other side of the page: faith was reckoned to Abraham for righteousness (Romans 4:9), and Paul then presses the timing — How was it then reckoned? when he was in circumcision, or in uncircumcision? Not in circumcision, but in uncircumcision (Romans 4:10). The entry was made before the sign was given, which shuts out every scheme that makes a rite or a work the ground. The same verb does the darkest and the sweetest work in Scripture. Isaiah’s Servant was reckoned among the transgressors, and the Lord Jesus quotes it of Himself the night He was taken (Luke 22:37) — the sinless One entered on the sinners’ page, so that sinners might be entered on His. And Paul turns the same accounting toward affliction: I reckon that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us (Romans 8:18).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines RECKON as to count, to number, to compute, to esteem, to account, to charge to an account, and to call to account. Every one of those senses is at work in Romans 4, where the noun is a debt, the verb is an entry, and the account belongs to God.
webster_full: RECKON, v.t. — To count; to number; that is, to tell the units of a sum.
To esteem; to account; to repute; as, he was reckoned among the transgressors.
To charge to an account; to place to the account of; to assign as a debt or a credit.
RECKON, v.i. — To settle accounts; to call to account; as, after a long time the lord of those servants cometh, and reckoneth with them (Matthew 25:19).
Webster’s commercial senses are exactly the ones Paul exploits: the reward reckoned of debt, and the righteousness reckoned of grace.
scriptures: Romans 4:4
Now to him that worketh is the reward not reckoned of grace, but of debt.
Romans 4:9
Cometh this blessedness then upon the circumcision only, or upon the uncircumcision also? for we say that faith was reckoned to Abraham for righteousness.
Romans 4:10
How was it then reckoned? when he was in circumcision, or in uncircumcision? Not in circumcision, but in uncircumcision.
Luke 22:37
For I say unto you, that this that is written must yet be accomplished in me, And he was reckoned among the transgressors: for the things concerning me have an end.
Romans 8:18
For I reckon that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us.
corruption_summary: The New Perspective on Paul empties the reckoning language of its forensic content, making justification a declaration of covenant membership rather than the crediting of an alien righteousness — which is precisely the transaction Romans 4:4 describes.
corruption_paragraphs: N. T. Wright and the New Perspective read Paul’s justification language as chiefly about who belongs to the covenant family and whether Gentiles must take on the Jewish badges. There is a real historical observation buried in that, but it will not carry Romans 4. Paul’s controlling contrast in verse 4 is not Jew against Gentile; it is grace against debt, and both are accounting terms. He then produces David as his second witness, quoting a psalm about a man whose sins are covered and to whom the Lord will not impute sin — a statement about guilt and its non-reckoning, not about table fellowship. The Reformed doctrine is the plain reading: Christ’s active and passive obedience is credited to the believer, and the believer’s sin was credited to Christ, who was reckoned among the transgressors.

The second corruption is homelier and more common in evangelical pulpits: the treatment of faith itself as the thing God accepts in place of righteousness, as though God graded on a curve and counted trusting as good enough. That is not what the text says either. Faith was reckoned for righteousness because faith lays hold of Another’s righteousness; the instrument is not the ground. Turretin and Owen both press this because it is where assurance lives. If God reckons my faith as my righteousness, then my assurance rests on the quality of my believing, which fluctuates hourly. If He reckons Christ’s righteousness to me and faith is the empty hand receiving it, then my standing is as steady as Christ.
roots_summary: Greek logizomai (G3049), to reckon, count, impute — the accountant’s verb, used eleven times in Romans 4; Hebrew chashab (H2803) is its counterpart in Genesis 15:6.
roots_lines: Greek logizomai (G3049) — to reckon, count, credit to an account; Romans 4:4, 4:9, 4:10, 8:18.
Hebrew chashab (H2803) — to think, to account, to impute; he counted it to him for righteousness (Genesis 15:6).
Greek ellogeo (G1677) — to charge to one’s account; put that on mine account (Philemon 18), the same idea in Paul’s own hand.
Greek opheilema (G3783) — a debt, that which is owed; the alternative Paul rules out in Romans 4:4.
Greek logizomai is also the verb behind reckon ye also yourselves to be dead indeed unto sin (Romans 6:11) — sanctification reasoning from a fact, not manufacturing one.
usage: The reward not reckoned of grace, but of debt (Romans 4:4) — the whole gospel turning on a bookkeeping distinction.
He was reckoned among the transgressors (Luke 22:37) — the great exchange stated in the ledger’s language.
I reckon that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared (Romans 8:18) — the same verb applied to affliction.

etymology: From Latin satis, enough, and facere, to make — to make enough. Webster 1828: to gratify wants, wishes or desires to the full extent; to free from doubt; to pay to content. The theological weight of the word is in Isaiah 53:11, where it is the Servant who is satisfied, and in the Reformed doctrine of satisfaction that answers to it.
biblical_def: Satisfied in Scripture is almost always a verdict on where a soul has looked for its fill. The negative case is stated as a law of nature: Hell and destruction are never full; so the eyes of man are never satisfied (Proverbs 27:20). Ecclesiastes says the same of money, and the whole book is an experiment proving it. Against that stands the psalmist’s single answer, which is not a different quantity but a different object: I shall be satisfied, when I awake, with thy likeness (Psalm 17:15). Not with plenty, not with vindication, and not in this life — when I awake, with Thy likeness. The table of the covenant meets it in this world in part: My soul shall be satisfied as with marrow and fatness (Psalm 63:5), and the meek shall eat and be satisfied (Psalm 22:26), a verse from the psalm of the cross. And underneath all of it lies the sentence that governs the doctrine of the atonement: He shall see of the travail of his soul, and shall be satisfied: by his knowledge shall my righteous servant justify many; for he shall bear their iniquities (Isaiah 53:11). The satisfaction of the Servant is the ground of every other satisfaction Scripture offers a sinner.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines SATISFY as to gratify wants or desires to the full; to supply fully; to free from doubt or suspense; and, in law and divinity, to pay or discharge a debt or penalty — the sense that gives the Reformed doctrine of satisfaction its name.
webster_full: SATISFY, v.t. — To gratify wants, wishes or desires to the full extent; to supply fully what is desired.
To free from doubt, suspense or uncertainty; to convince, as by evidence.
To pay to content; to discharge, as a claim or a penalty; to make satisfaction for an offense.
SATISFACTION, n. — That which satisfies; amends; atonement for a crime; the payment of a penalty due.
Webster’s legal sense is the one Anselm and the Reformed divines use: Christ’s death is a satisfaction to divine justice, not merely an influence upon men.
scriptures: Isaiah 53:11
He shall see of the travail of his soul, and shall be satisfied: by his knowledge shall my righteous servant justify many; for he shall bear their iniquities.
Psalm 17:15
As for me, I will behold thy face in righteousness: I shall be satisfied, when I awake, with thy likeness.
Psalm 22:26
The meek shall eat and be satisfied: they shall praise the LORD that seek him: your heart shall live for ever.
Psalm 63:5
My soul shall be satisfied as with marrow and fatness; and my mouth shall praise thee with joyful lips:
Proverbs 27:20
Hell and destruction are never full; so the eyes of man are never satisfied.
corruption_summary: Satisfaction has been relocated from God to the self. The modern question is whether a man is satisfied with his life; Scripture’s question is whether God has been satisfied concerning his sin, and the answer at Calvary settles the other one.
corruption_paragraphs: Therapeutic religion treats satisfaction as an internal state to be cultivated: contentment practices, gratitude exercises, the management of expectation. Some of that is common-sense wisdom and Scripture has its own version of it, since Paul learned in whatsoever state he was therewith to be content. But Proverbs 27:20 says the eye cannot be trained to be full, because the appetite is not a habit but a hunger, and hell itself is the standard of comparison. No discipline satisfies an infinite capacity with finite objects. Psalm 17:15 answers with an object rather than a technique, and defers the fulness to the resurrection: when I awake, with thy likeness. Any spirituality that promises the fulness now, without the waking, is promising what the psalmist did not.

The graver corruption is the loss of the objective doctrine. Modern theories of the atonement — moral influence, Christus Victor made exclusive, governmental theories — all move the transaction away from God’s justice being satisfied and toward something happening in man or in the cosmos. Isaiah 53:11 has the Servant satisfied at the sight of the travail of His soul, and the reason given is that he shall bear their iniquities. Sin was borne, justice was answered, and the One who bore it is content with what He purchased. That is why the doctrine of definite atonement matters pastorally: a satisfaction actually rendered for actual persons is a finished thing, and the believer’s peace rests on a completed payment rather than on a possibility.
roots_summary: Hebrew saba (H7646), to be sated or filled; Greek chortazo (G5526), to feed to the full; the doctrinal noun is Latin satisfactio, a making-enough.
roots_lines: Hebrew saba (H7646) — to be satisfied, sated, filled; Psalm 17:15, 22:26, 63:5, Proverbs 27:20.
Hebrew sobah (H7648) — satiety, fulness; the noun of the same root.
Greek chortazo (G5526) — to feed, to fill; Blessed are they which do hunger and thirst after righteousness: for they shall be filled (Matthew 5:6).
Latin satis facere — to make enough; whence satisfaction, the classical Reformed term for Christ’s work Godward.
Isaiah 53:11 reads literally that from the travail of His soul He shall see and be satisfied — the Servant’s own contentment with the result of His suffering.
usage: He shall see of the travail of his soul, and shall be satisfied (Isaiah 53:11) — the Servant content with what His death purchased.
I shall be satisfied, when I awake, with thy likeness (Psalm 17:15) — fulness deferred to the resurrection.
The eyes of man are never satisfied (Proverbs 27:20) — the appetite measured against hell.

etymology: From Latin jungere, to yoke, through Old French joindre; the same root as yoke and conjugal. Webster 1828: to set or bring one thing in contiguity with another; to unite; to associate. Scripture uses it for the three unions that decide a life — marriage, idolatry, and Christ.
biblical_def: Joined is a covenant verb. Our Lord takes Genesis 2:24 and puts the joining in God’s hands, not the couple’s: What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder (Matthew 19:6). Marriage is not a partnership two people assemble and may therefore disassemble; it is a union God makes, and that is why divorce is presented as sundering something rather than ending an arrangement. Paul then applies the same word in two directions in a single passage. He which is joined to an harlot is one body (1 Corinthians 6:16) — fornication is not a private transaction with no metaphysics; it makes a union, and that is the horror of it. And immediately, he that is joined unto the Lord is one spirit (1 Corinthians 6:17), which is the reason the first is unthinkable. The Old Testament uses the verb for the worst of Israel’s sins: Israel joined himself unto Baalpeor (Numbers 25:3), and Hosea’s terrible verdict, Ephraim is joined to idols: let him alone (Hosea 4:17). Man is a joining creature; the only question the Bible entertains is what he will be joined to.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines JOIN as to set or bring together, to unite in league or marriage, to associate, to couple, to add. The marriage sense he illustrates from Matthew 19:6, and the older English idiom to join battle preserves the sense of closing with an enemy.
webster_full: JOIN, v.t. — To set or bring one thing in contiguity with another; to couple; to connect; to combine.
To unite in marriage; as, what God hath joined together, let no man put asunder.
To associate; to unite with in league or confederacy; as, to join an army, to join a church.
To join battle — to begin an engagement; a phrase Webster notes from the older histories.
The Latin jungere gives also yoke, which is why the New Testament can move between being joined to Christ and taking His yoke.
scriptures: Genesis 2:24
Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.
Matthew 19:6
Wherefore they are no more twain, but one flesh. What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder.
1 Corinthians 6:16
What? know ye not that he which is joined to an harlot is one body? for two, saith he, shall be one flesh.
1 Corinthians 6:17
But he that is joined unto the Lord is one spirit.
Hosea 4:17
Ephraim is joined to idols: let him alone.
corruption_summary: Marriage has been redefined from a union God makes to a contract two adults negotiate, which is exactly the premise Matthew 19:6 denies; and the hookup culture rests on the denial of 1 Corinthians 6:16, that a body can be joined without anything being joined.
corruption_paragraphs: The contractual view of marriage is now the assumed one, and it produces the rest by simple logic: if two parties made the arrangement, two parties may unmake it; if the terms are theirs to write, the sexes of the parties are a term like any other. Christ forecloses all of it in one clause by identifying the agent. What therefore God hath joined together — the joining is a divine act performed upon a man and a woman, grounded in the creation ordinance He had just quoted, he which made them at the beginning made them male and female. Our Lord answered a first-century divorce debate by going behind Moses to Genesis, and the same method answers the twenty-first century’s questions. The creation order is not one voice in a conversation; it is the standing structure of the thing.

Paul’s argument in 1 Corinthians 6 is the one modern sexual ethics cannot absorb at all. The Corinthian slogan was that the body is morally indifferent — meats for the belly, and the belly for meats — and Paul answers that the body is for the Lord, that it is a member of Christ, and that the man who goes to a harlot has made a one-flesh union with her. There is no such thing as a merely physical act, because there is no such thing as a merely physical person. The remedy he gives is not a technique but a fact and a command: ye are not your own, for ye are bought with a price, therefore flee fornication. The doctrine of union with Christ is the reason chastity is possible, and Hosea’s let him alone is the warning of what God does with a people who will not be parted from their idols.
roots_summary: Hebrew tsamad (H6775), to bind or join, used of Baalpeor; chabar (H2266), to be joined or allied; Greek kollao (G2853), to glue or cement together.
roots_lines: Hebrew tsamad (H6775) — to bind, to join oneself to; Israel joined himself unto Baalpeor (Numbers 25:3).
Hebrew chabar (H2266) — to unite, to be joined, to be allied; Ephraim is joined to idols (Hosea 4:17).
Hebrew dabaq (H1692) — to cleave, to cling; shall cleave unto his wife (Genesis 2:24).
Greek kollao (G2853) — to glue, to cement, to join fast; 1 Corinthians 6:16-17 uses it of both unions.
Greek suzeugnumi (G4801) — to yoke together; the verb behind what God hath joined together (Matthew 19:6).
usage: What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder (Matthew 19:6) — the agent of marriage identified.
He that is joined unto the Lord is one spirit (1 Corinthians 6:17) — union with Christ stated in a single clause.
Ephraim is joined to idols: let him alone (Hosea 4:17) — the most terrifying sentence in the minor prophets.

etymology: From Latin occasio, from occidere, to fall down or befall — a thing that falls in one’s way. Webster 1828: occurrence; incident; opportunity; a favourable juncture. In the Authorized Version it renders a military word for a base of operations, and Paul uses it of what sin does with the law.
biblical_def: Occasion in the New Testament is chiefly Paul’s word for a bridgehead. Twice in Romans 7 he says that sin, taking occasion by the commandment, wrought concupiscence in him and deceived him and slew him (Romans 7:8, 11). The commandment was holy, just, and good; sin used it as a launching point, seizing on the prohibition to inflame the very desire forbidden. This is one of Scripture’s deepest observations about fallen nature, and every honest man recognizes it. Paul then puts the same word to the church’s use in three practical directions. Liberty is not to become a base for the flesh: use not liberty for an occasion to the flesh, but by love serve one another (Galatians 5:13). Christian conduct is to give the world nothing to work with: younger widows are to marry and guide the house and give none occasion to the adversary to speak reproachfully (1 Timothy 5:14). And in the fellowship, the strong brother is to judge this rather, that no man put a stumblingblock or an occasion to fall in his brother’s way (Romans 14:13). John gives the reverse and better case: He that loveth his brother abideth in the light, and there is none occasion of stumbling in him (1 John 2:10).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines OCCASION as occurrence, incident, casualty; opportunity; a favourable time or season; and, in the older usage, a cause or ground of action. The Latin sense of something falling in one’s way is the key to Paul’s use.
webster_full: OCCASION, n. — Occurrence; incident; accidental event; that which falls out or happens.
Opportunity; convenience; favorable juncture; as, to take occasion.
Incidental need; casual exigency; want at a particular time; as, the occasions of the poor.
That which gives rise or ground to something else; the immediate cause, distinguished by the older logicians from the efficient cause.
The scholastic distinction between a cause and an occasion is exactly what protects the law in Romans 7: the commandment was the occasion, indwelling sin was the cause.
scriptures: Romans 7:8
But sin, taking occasion by the commandment, wrought in me all manner of concupiscence. For without the law sin was dead.
Romans 7:11
For sin, taking occasion by the commandment, deceived me, and by it slew me.
Romans 14:13
Let us not therefore judge one another any more: but judge this rather, that no man put a stumblingblock or an occasion to fall in his brother’s way.
Galatians 5:13
For, brethren, ye have been called unto liberty; only use not liberty for an occasion to the flesh, but by love serve one another.
1 John 2:10
He that loveth his brother abideth in the light, and there is none occasion of stumbling in him.
corruption_summary: Romans 7:8 is the favourite proof text of everyone who wants to blame the law for sin — the antinomian, the sentimental permissivist, and the modern psychologist who treats prohibition itself as the source of disorder. Paul refutes all three in the next breath.
corruption_paragraphs: Having said that sin took occasion by the commandment, Paul immediately asks the obvious question and answers it with his strongest negative: Is the law sin? God forbid. He goes further — the law is holy, and the commandment holy, and just, and good — and then names the real culprit: that sin by the commandment might become exceeding sinful. The prohibition did not create the appetite; it exposed and provoked what was already there, the way a lamp does not create the filth in a room. This distinction is the difference between the Reformed doctrine of the law and the antinomianism that recurs in every generation. Rules do not manufacture rebels. They reveal them, and a nature that flares at a boundary is telling the truth about itself.

The therapeutic version of this error deserves naming, because it is now the ordinary parenting and pastoral advice of the age: that forbidding a thing makes it attractive, and that the wise course is therefore to forbid as little as possible. Scripture agrees about the mechanism and disagrees entirely about the conclusion. God gave the law knowing exactly what fallen men would do with it, because the law was never given to make men good; it was given, Galatians says, as a schoolmaster to bring us unto Christ. Removing the commandment does not remove the concupiscence; it only removes the diagnosis. The answer to Romans 7 is not fewer commandments but Romans 8, and a nature made new.
roots_summary: Greek aphorme (G874), a starting point, a base of operations from which an attack is made; also proskomma and skandalon for the stumbling sense in Romans 14:13.
roots_lines: Greek aphorme (G874) — a base of operations, a starting point for an expedition; Romans 7:8, 11; Galatians 5:13; 1 Timothy 5:14.
Greek skandalon (G4625) — the trigger of a trap, an occasion of stumbling; Romans 14:13 and 1 John 2:10.
Greek proskomma (G4348) — a stumblingblock, something struck against; paired with skandalon in Romans 14:13.
Greek epithumia (G1939) — strong desire, concupiscence; what sin wrought by the occasion of the tenth commandment.
The military flavour of aphorme is deliberate: sin does not merely notice the commandment, it uses it as ground from which to mount an assault.
usage: Sin, taking occasion by the commandment (Romans 7:8) — the law as the bridgehead indwelling sin exploits.
Use not liberty for an occasion to the flesh (Galatians 5:13) — Christian freedom fenced against its own abuse.
There is none occasion of stumbling in him (1 John 2:10) — the man who loves his brother gives sin no ground.

etymology: From Old English lufu, love. Webster 1828 gives LOVER as one who loves, one who has a tender affection, and notes the older and broader English sense — a lover of learning, a lover of his country. The Authorized Version keeps that breadth, which is why 2 Timothy 3 can list what a man loves as the index of what he is.
biblical_def: Lovers in the Authorized Version is rarely romantic and almost always diagnostic. Paul’s catalogue of the last days is built on the word: men shall be lovers of their own selves, covetous, boasters, proud (2 Timothy 3:2), and the list closes with the sentence that names the whole disorder — lovers of pleasures more than lovers of God (2 Timothy 3:4). The structure is deliberate. The chapter begins with self-love and ends with pleasure-love, and everything vicious between the two is what self-love produces when it is fed. Notice that Paul does not say these men love no God at all; he says the affections are wrongly ranked, and adds that they have a form of godliness. The qualifications for an elder use the same word positively: he must be a lover of hospitality, a lover of good men (Titus 1:8). And David uses it of ordinary human company in the loneliest verse of the psalms of affliction: My lovers and my friends stand aloof from my sore; and my kinsmen stand afar off (Psalm 38:11). Scripture’s consistent assumption is that every man is a lover of something. Sanctification is not the removal of the affections but their reordering.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines LOVER as one who loves; one who has a tender affection, particularly for a female; and, more generally, one who likes or is well pleased with anything — a lover of his country, a lover of books. The Authorized Version uses the wider sense throughout.
webster_full: LOVER, n. — One who loves; one who has a tender affection.
One who is in love; a suitor; the sense that has since crowded out the others in ordinary English.
A friend; one who regards with kindness; as, my lovers and my friends stand aloof (Psalm 38:11).
One who likes or is pleased with anything; as, a lover of peace, a lover of hospitality (Titus 1:8).
The narrowing of the English word since 1828 obscures Paul’s point: lovers of pleasures more than lovers of God is a statement about the ordering of all a man’s affections, not about romance.
scriptures: 2 Timothy 3:2
For men shall be lovers of their own selves, covetous, boasters, proud, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, unthankful, unholy,
2 Timothy 3:4
Traitors, heady, highminded, lovers of pleasures more than lovers of God;
Titus 1:8
But a lover of hospitality, a lover of good men, sober, just, holy, temperate;
Psalm 38:11
My lovers and my friends stand aloof from my sore; and my kinsmen stand afar off.
Hosea 4:17
Ephraim is joined to idols: let him alone.
corruption_summary: Self-love, which Paul heads the list of the last days’ corruptions, has been rebranded as self-care, self-compassion, and the necessary precondition of loving others — and taught as such from pulpits that would otherwise call themselves conservative.
corruption_paragraphs: The teaching that a man must love himself before he can love his neighbour is now so common that quoting 2 Timothy 3:2 against it sounds eccentric. It rests on a misreading of the second great commandment: thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself assumes self-love as a given, the way the golden rule assumes you already know what you would want done to you. It does not command it. Calvin, Augustine, and the whole older tradition agree that self-love is the constant and the problem, not the deficiency. The therapeutic vocabulary — self-care, self-compassion, honouring your needs — is not simply worldly language for a biblical idea; it inverts the diagnosis. The gospel’s cure for a man curved in upon himself is not a better opinion of himself but a sight of Christ.

The parallel error, softer and no less serious, is the treatment of pleasure as the enemy. Paul does not say lovers of pleasures full stop; he says more than lovers of God. Scripture is not ascetic. It gives wine that maketh glad the heart of man, a feast that God commands, a Song of Solomon in the canon, and pleasures at God’s right hand for evermore. The corruption is a ranking, not an appetite. That is why the Puritans, who are caricatured as the enemies of enjoyment, wrote so much about delight in God: they understood that a disordered affection is not defeated by being starved but by being outbid.
roots_summary: Greek philautos (G5367), self-loving; philedonos (G5369), pleasure-loving; philotheos (G5377), God-loving — three compounds of phileo that Paul sets against each other.
roots_lines: Greek philautos (G5367) — lovers of their own selves; a hapax legomenon at 2 Timothy 3:2.
Greek philedonos (G5369) — lovers of pleasure; 2 Timothy 3:4, set directly against the next word.
Greek philotheos (G5377) — lovers of God; also a hapax, occurring only in that same verse.
Greek philoxenos (G5382) — a lover of hospitality, literally a lover of strangers; required of an elder (Titus 1:8).
Hebrew ahab (H157) — to love; the participle gives my lovers in Psalm 38:11 in the sense of friends.
usage: Lovers of their own selves (2 Timothy 3:2) — the head of Paul’s list of last-days corruptions.
Lovers of pleasures more than lovers of God (2 Timothy 3:4) — a disorder of ranking, not of appetite.
A lover of hospitality, a lover of good men (Titus 1:8) — the same word in an elder’s qualifications.

etymology: From Old English beatan, to strike. Webster 1828 gives, among the senses of BEATEN, hammered; formed by beating, and worn by treading, as a beaten path. Scripture uses both: the sanctuary’s holiest furniture was beaten work, and the servants and apostles of God were beaten men.
biblical_def: Beaten runs through Scripture along two lines that meet at the cross. The first is craftsmanship. The cherubim over the mercy seat were not cast or joined: of beaten work shalt thou make them, in the two ends of the mercy seat (Exodus 25:18), hammered out of the same piece as the lid. The candlestick likewise was of beaten gold… according unto the pattern which the LORD had shewed Moses (Numbers 8:4). And the light in the holy place burned on pure oil olive beaten for the light (Exodus 27:20) — oil pressed by hand from the first crushing of the fruit, the costliest and clearest grade. Every visible glory of the sanctuary was made by hammering and crushing. The second line is suffering. That servant, which knew his lord’s will, and prepared not himself… shall be beaten with many stripes (Luke 12:47), a warning of degrees in judgment. Paul counts his beatings among his credentials: Thrice was I beaten with rods (2 Corinthians 11:25), and at Philippi, They have beaten us openly uncondemned, being Romans (Acts 16:37). Isaiah’s Servant was beaten before either apostle was, and the gold of the sanctuary was always a picture of it.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 lists for BEATEN: hammered, formed by beating; worn by use or by treading, as a beaten road; and, figuratively, worn out or exhausted. The first sense is the sanctuary’s, the second is the proverb’s, and Scripture uses both.
webster_full: BEATEN, pp. — Struck; dashed against; pounded; conquered; worn by treading.
Hammered; formed by beating; as beaten gold, beaten work — the technical term for metal shaped by the hammer rather than cast in a mould.
Made smooth or hard by treading; as a beaten path, a beaten track.
BEATEN OIL — oil obtained by pounding olives in a mortar rather than by pressing them in the mill; the purest sort, appointed for the lamp (Exodus 27:20).
Webster’s technical distinction matters: a cast image is poured into a shape by another’s design, but beaten work is drawn out of solid metal by long, patient blows.
scriptures: Exodus 25:18
And thou shalt make two cherubims of gold, of beaten work shalt thou make them, in the two ends of the mercy seat.
Numbers 8:4

And this work of the candlestick was of beaten gold, unto the shaft thereof, unto the flowers thereof, was beaten work: according unto the pattern which the LORD had shewed Moses, so he made the candlestick.
Exodus 37:7
And he made two cherubims of gold, beaten out of one piece made he them, on the two ends of the mercy seat;
Luke 12:47
And that servant, which knew his lord’s will, and prepared not himself, neither did according to his will, shall be beaten with many stripes.
2 Corinthians 11:25
Thrice was I beaten with rods, once was I stoned, thrice I suffered shipwreck, a night and a day I have been in the deep;
corruption_summary: Luke 12:47 teaches degrees of punishment in hell, and it is quietly dropped by two opposite parties — those who deny hell altogether, and those who preach it so flatly that Scripture’s own distinctions disappear.
corruption_paragraphs: Our Lord says the servant who knew his lord’s will and did it not shall be beaten with many stripes, and the one who knew not and did commit things worthy of stripes shall be beaten with few. The passage closes, unto whomsoever much is given, of him shall be much required. The Reformed tradition has always taught degrees of punishment on the strength of this and of Matthew 11:22 about Tyre and Sidon, and it is a doctrine with a sharp edge for the churched. Sitting under faithful preaching is not a neutral condition. It raises the account. The man who has heard the gospel plainly for thirty years and never bowed is not in the position of the man who has never heard it, and he is not in a better one.

The sanctuary line of the word yields the other lesson, and it is a comfort rather than a warning. Everything that gave light or covered the mercy seat was made by beating: the cherubim hammered out of the same gold as the lid they overshadowed, the candlestick beaten from shaft to flower, the oil pounded from the olive. Nothing in the holy place was cast quickly in a mould. God’s ordinary method with what He intends to make beautiful and useful is long, repeated pressure, and Scripture says so plainly enough that no believer should read his afflictions as evidence of neglect. The trial of your faith, being much more precious than of gold that perisheth, though it be tried with fire.
roots_summary: Hebrew miqshah (H4749), beaten work, hammered out of one piece; kathith (H3795), beaten or pounded, of the oil; Greek dero (G1194), to flay or beat, and rhabdizo (G4463), to beat with rods.
roots_lines: Hebrew miqshah (H4749) — beaten work, of one piece; the cherubim and the candlestick (Exodus 25:18; Numbers 8:4).
Hebrew kathith (H3795) — beaten, pounded; of the pure olive oil for the lamp (Exodus 27:20).
Greek dero (G1194) — to flay, to beat; beaten with many stripes (Luke 12:47).
Greek rhabdizo (G4463) — to beat with rods; the Roman punishment Paul suffered thrice (2 Corinthians 11:25; Acts 16:22).
Greek plege (G4127) — a stripe, a blow; the noun behind many stripes and few stripes.
usage: Of beaten work shalt thou make them (Exodus 25:18) — the cherubim hammered from the mercy seat’s own gold.
Pure oil olive beaten for the light (Exodus 27:20) — the crushed first pressing appointed for the lamp.
Shall be beaten with many stripes (Luke 12:47) — degrees of punishment, taught by Christ.

etymology: From maze, a bewilderment or labyrinth; the Old English sense is to stupefy, to confound. Webster 1828: astonished; confounded with fear, surprise or wonder. In the Gospels it is the standing reaction of the crowds to Christ, and once it is used of Christ Himself in Gethsemane.
biblical_def: Amazed is Mark’s word above all, and it describes something stronger than admiration. At Capernaum, after the unclean spirit came out, they were all amazed, insomuch that they questioned among themselves, saying, What thing is this? what new doctrine is this? for with authority commandeth he even the unclean spirits, and they do obey him (Mark 1:27). The amazement is not at a miracle in the abstract but at authority; the crowd is trying to place a category of person they have never met. Luke records the same after the palsied man rose: they were all amazed, and they glorified God, and were filled with fear, saying, We have seen strange things to day (Luke 5:26). Amazement in the Gospels is regularly joined to fear, and it is not the same thing as faith — the same crowds that were amazed also cried, Crucify him. The most solemn use is Gethsemane: he taketh with him Peter and James and John, and began to be sore amazed, and to be very heavy (Mark 14:33). The Greek is strong, and the King James translators did not soften it. The Son of God, going to bear the wrath He had known from eternity was coming, was struck with a horror His humanity felt to the full.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines AMAZED as astonished, confounded with fear, surprise or wonder; and AMAZEMENT as astonishment, confusion, perplexity arising from terror or wonder. The older English kept the element of terror the modern word has lost.
webster_full: AMAZED, pp. — Astonished; confounded with fear, surprise or admiration.
AMAZEMENT, n. — Astonishment; confusion; perplexity arising from a sudden impression of terror, or from an object of wonder.
The root is maze, a state of bewilderment, as one lost in a labyrinth; the original force is disorientation, not delight.
Webster notes that the word formerly implied terror more strongly than in his own day — a drift that has continued, so that amazing is now nearly a compliment.
This drift matters for reading Mark 14:33: sore amazed in 1611 English meant something close to struck with horror.
scriptures: Mark 1:27

And they were all amazed, insomuch that they questioned among themselves, saying, What thing is this? what new doctrine is this? for with authority commandeth he even the unclean spirits, and they do obey him.
Mark 10:32

And they were in the way going up to Jerusalem; and Jesus went before them: and they were amazed; and as they followed, they were afraid. And he took again the twelve, and began to tell them what things should happen unto him,
Luke 5:26
And they were all amazed, and they glorified God, and were filled with fear, saying, We have seen strange things to day.
Mark 14:33
And he taketh with him Peter and James and John, and began to be sore amazed, and to be very heavy;
Acts 3:10
And they knew that it was he which sat for alms at the Beautiful gate of the temple: and they were filled with wonder and amazement at that which had happened unto him.
corruption_summary: Modern worship aims at amazement and calls it encounter, but the Gospels are careful to distinguish amazement from faith: the amazed crowds are the same crowds that afterward wanted Him dead.
corruption_paragraphs: Mark records amazement constantly and conversion rarely. The crowds are astonished at His doctrine, astonished at His authority, astonished beyond measure at the healing of the deaf man, and the same city that thronged Him is the one where the multitude is persuaded to ask for Barabbas. Amazement is a response of the affections to power, and fallen affections respond to power without submitting to it. This is worth saying plainly wherever corporate worship is designed to produce a peak emotional experience and that experience is then treated as evidence of the Spirit’s work. The regulative principle asks a different question of a service: not whether the people were moved, but whether God was worshipped as He commanded. Faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God.

Mark 14:33 must not be softened, and the classical doctrine is what keeps it from being distorted in either direction. The Chalcedonian confession holds two natures in one Person, without confusion and without division. The horror in Gethsemane is real and is felt in the human nature the Son assumed; the divine nature is impassible and does not suffer change. This is not a technicality. It is what allows a Christian to say both that his Saviour truly knows dread — sore amazed, very heavy, sweating as it were great drops of blood — and that the God on whom he leans is not Himself shaken. Take away either half and the comfort collapses.
roots_summary: Greek existemi (G1839), to stand out of oneself, to be beside oneself; thambeo (G2284) and ekthambeo (G1568), to be struck with awe or terror — the latter used of Christ in Gethsemane.
roots_lines: Greek thambeo (G2284) — to be astounded, struck with awe; they were all amazed (Mark 1:27).
Greek ekthambeo (G1568) — to be greatly amazed, struck with terror; sore amazed (Mark 14:33).
Greek existemi (G1839) — to displace, to be beside oneself; they were all amazed (Luke 5:26).
Greek ekstasis (G1611) — amazement, a standing outside oneself; filled with wonder and amazement (Acts 3:10).
Greek ademoneo (G85) — to be in distress or heaviness; the companion word in Mark 14:33, very heavy.
usage: What new doctrine is this? (Mark 1:27) — amazement at authority, not merely at power.
They were amazed; and as they followed, they were afraid (Mark 10:32) — the disciples on the road to Jerusalem.
Began to be sore amazed, and to be very heavy (Mark 14:33) — the word the translators would not soften.

etymology: From Old French plaisant, from Latin placere, to please. Webster 1828: pleasing; agreeable; grateful to the mind or to the senses. In Scripture it is a two-edged word: the first sin was pleasant to the eyes, and the believer’s inheritance falls in pleasant places.
biblical_def: Pleasant is one of Scripture’s most carefully balanced words, because it is used of the bait and of the blessing with equal frankness. The fall turns on it: when the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was pleasant to the eyes, and a tree to be desired to make one wise, she took of the fruit thereof, and did eat (Genesis 3:6) — three appeals, of which the middle is bare pleasantness. John’s lust of the eyes is a summary of that clause. Yet Scripture never concludes from this that pleasantness is suspect in itself, because God is the author of it. The believer’s portion is described in exactly the same terms: The lines are fallen unto me in pleasant places; yea, I have a goodly heritage (Psalm 16:6), a psalm that ends in resurrection and pleasures for evermore. Solomon commends good speech in the same key: Pleasant words are as an honeycomb, sweet to the soul, and health to the bones (Proverbs 16:24). David’s elegy over Saul and Jonathan calls them lovely and pleasant in their lives (2 Samuel 1:23) — generous language about a king who had hunted him. And the great verse on the unity of brethren stands on it: Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity! (Psalm 133:1).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines PLEASANT as pleasing, agreeable, grateful to the mind or to the senses; cheerful, enlivening; and, in a lower sense, trifling or merry. The mixture of high and low in his own entry answers to the mixture in Scripture’s usage.
webster_full: PLEASANT, a. — Pleasing; agreeable; grateful to the mind or to the senses; as a pleasant prospect, a pleasant taste.
Cheerful; enlivening; as pleasant company, a pleasant countenance.
Gay; lively; humorous; sportive; sometimes with the implication of trifling.
Trifling; adapted rather to mirth than to use — a sense Webster marks as inferior and now nearly obsolete.
From Latin placere, to please, whence also placid, complacent, and please itself.
scriptures: Genesis 3:6

And when the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was pleasant to the eyes, and a tree to be desired to make one wise, she took of the fruit thereof, and did eat, and gave also unto her husband with her; and he did eat.
Psalm 16:6
The lines are fallen unto me in pleasant places; yea, I have a goodly heritage.
Psalm 133:1
Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!
Proverbs 16:24
Pleasant words are as an honeycomb, sweet to the soul, and health to the bones.
2 Samuel 1:23
Saul and Jonathan were lovely and pleasant in their lives, and in their death they were not divided: they were swifter than eagles, they were stronger than lions.
corruption_summary: Pleasantness has been promoted from a good thing to the governing test of a message, so that a doctrine’s pleasantness is now widely treated as evidence of its truth — the exact reasoning of Genesis 3:6.
corruption_paragraphs: Eve saw that the tree was pleasant to the eyes. The narrative records her reasoning in full and does not say she was stupid; she assessed the fruit by appetite, appearance, and promised benefit, which is how every unbeliever assesses every claim. The modern form of it is the assumption that a hard doctrine is thereby probably false — that a God who elects, or who judges, or who has fixed the boundaries of marriage, cannot be the real one because such a God is unpleasant. Isaiah described the market for that precisely: speak unto us smooth things, prophesy deceits. The corrective is not a taste for grim doctrine. It is the recognition that pleasantness is a quality of things, not a test of them, and that the serpent’s whole method was to make the forbidden look better than the given.

The opposite error is a sour Christianity that treats every pleasure as a snare, and Scripture gives it no support at all. Psalm 16, which David wrote and Peter preached at Pentecost as a prophecy of the resurrection, contains the lines are fallen unto me in pleasant places and ends with at thy right hand there are pleasures for evermore. Psalm 133 calls the unity of brethren pleasant and compares it to the anointing oil running down Aaron’s beard. Proverbs commends pleasant words as honeycomb and health to the bones. A Christian who cannot say of his own portion that the lines have fallen in pleasant places has usually mistaken ingratitude for seriousness.
roots_summary: Hebrew naim (H5273), pleasant, delightful, from naem (H5276), to be sweet or agreeable — the root behind the name Naomi; and ta’avah, desire, in Genesis 3:6.
roots_lines: Hebrew naim (H5273) — pleasant, delightful, sweet; Psalm 16:6, 133:1, 2 Samuel 1:23.
Hebrew naem (H5276) — to be pleasant, agreeable; the root of Naomi, my pleasantness (Ruth 1:20).
Hebrew ta’avah (H8378) — desire, longing; pleasant to the eyes in Genesis 3:6 renders a related idea of what draws the eye.
Hebrew chemdah (H2532) — desirable, precious; used of the pleasant land in Jeremiah 3:19 and Zechariah 7:14.
Greek hedus — sweet, pleasant; the root of hedone, pleasure, and of philedonos, lovers of pleasure (2 Timothy 3:4).
usage: Pleasant to the eyes, and a tree to be desired (Genesis 3:6) — the assessment that lost Eden.
The lines are fallen unto me in pleasant places (Psalm 16:6) — the believer’s estimate of his own portion.
How good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity (Psalm 133:1) — pleasantness as a mark of the church.

etymology: From Old English weorc, work. Webster 1828: one who works; one who is employed in labour. In the Authorized Version the plural almost always carries a qualifier that decides everything — workers of iniquity, deceitful workers, evil workers, or workers together with God.
biblical_def: Workers in Scripture is never a neutral occupational term; it is always followed by the word that judges it. The most frequent phrase in the Psalms is workers of iniquity, the standing description of the wicked as men actively employed at their sin: Depart from me, all ye workers of iniquity; for the LORD hath heard the voice of my weeping (Psalm 6:8) — a line the Lord Jesus takes up in the most terrible sentence of the Sermon on the Mount, I never knew you: depart from me, ye that work iniquity. Paul uses the plural three times of false teachers. They are deceitful workers, transforming themselves into the apostles of Christ (2 Corinthians 11:13), and the church is warned, Beware of dogs, beware of evil workers, beware of the concision (Philippians 3:2). Against all of these stands the one glorious use: We then, as workers together with him, beseech you also that ye receive not the grace of God in vain (2 Corinthians 6:1). The category is not labour against idleness. Every man in Scripture is a worker. The question the word puts is whose work he is doing, and the answer at the last day is announced in exactly these terms.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines WORKER simply as one that works, one that performs labour. Scripture’s usage adds nothing to the definition and everything to the description, since the noun in the Authorized Version is nearly always governed by a genitive that fixes its moral character.
webster_full: WORKER, n. — One who works; one that performs labour or is employed in any occupation.

In Scripture the noun is characteristically qualified: workers of iniquity (Psalm 6:8), deceitful workers (2 Corinthians 11:13), evil workers (Philippians 3:2), workers together with God (2 Corinthians 6:1).
The Old English weorc gives also wright, as in wheelwright and shipwright, and stands behind the New Testament word for a craftsman.
The related word workman appears in the charge to Timothy: a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth (2 Timothy 2:15).
Webster’s spare entry is itself instructive: the English word carries no moral content, and Scripture supplies it every time.
scriptures: Psalm 6:8
Depart from me, all ye workers of iniquity; for the LORD hath heard the voice of my weeping.
Matthew 7:23
And then will I profess unto them, I never knew you: depart from me, ye that work iniquity.
2 Corinthians 6:1
We then, as workers together with him, beseech you also that ye receive not the grace of God in vain.
2 Corinthians 11:13
For such are false apostles, deceitful workers, transforming themselves into the apostles of Christ.
Philippians 3:2
Beware of dogs, beware of evil workers, beware of the concision.
corruption_summary: Matthew 7:23 is addressed to men who prophesied, cast out devils, and did many wonderful works in Christ’s name — and the modern church, which measures ministry by exactly those outputs, has almost no category for the warning.
corruption_paragraphs: The men in Matthew 7:22 are not scoffers. They present a ministry record: prophecy, exorcism, many wonderful works, all in the name of Christ. The Lord does not dispute a single item on the list. He says, I never knew you — not I knew you and you fell away, but I never knew you — and He classifies the whole ministry as working iniquity. This is the strongest possible refutation of the idea that effectiveness authenticates a servant. It is also the reason the Reformed tradition has insisted on the marks of a true church and the necessity of regeneration in ministers as well as members. A man may have gifts without grace. Gifts are given for the church’s benefit; grace is given for the man’s salvation, and God has never obliged Himself to give both to the same person.

Paul’s workers together with him supplies the counterweight before the doctrine curdles into paralysis. The apostle who could not tolerate deceitful workers describes his own ministry as labouring alongside God, and elsewhere as labouring more abundantly than they all: yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me. That is the Reformed doctrine of concurrence applied to Christian service: real human labour, genuinely willed and genuinely exerting, and God the whole cause of whatever comes of it. The believer works out his own salvation with fear and trembling precisely because it is God which worketh in him both to will and to do.
roots_summary: Hebrew poalei aven, workers of iniquity, from paal (H6466) to do or make and aven (H205) vanity or wickedness; Greek ergates (G2040), a workman or labourer.
roots_lines: Hebrew paal (H6466) — to do, to make, to work; the participle gives workers in the Psalms.
Hebrew aven (H205) — vanity, nothingness, iniquity; the object in workers of iniquity (Psalm 6:8).
Greek ergates (G2040) — a workman, labourer; deceitful workers (2 Corinthians 11:13), evil workers (Philippians 3:2), and the labourer is worthy of his hire.
Greek sunergeo (G4903) — to work together with; the verb behind workers together with him (2 Corinthians 6:1).
Greek anomia (G458) — lawlessness, iniquity; ye that work iniquity (Matthew 7:23) is literally ye that work lawlessness.
usage: Depart from me, all ye workers of iniquity (Psalm 6:8) — the phrase Christ takes up at the judgment.
Deceitful workers, transforming themselves into the apostles of Christ (2 Corinthians 11:13) — false ministry named.
Workers together with him (2 Corinthians 6:1) — the one wholly good use of the plural.

etymology: From Old English teogotha, tenth, the same root that gives tithe. Webster 1828 defines TENTH as the ordinal of ten, and notes that the tenth part is the tithe. In Scripture the word does double service: it names the portion given to God, and it names the remnant God leaves.
biblical_def: The tenth is Scripture’s appointed proportion and its picture of a remnant. It appears before the law, in Abraham’s dealing with Melchizedek: he gave him tithes of all (Genesis 14:20), which Hebrews expounds as Abraham gave a tenth part of all (Hebrews 7:2) and then presses into an argument about a priesthood greater than Levi’s — consider how great this man was, unto whom even the patriarch Abraham gave the tenth of the spoils (Hebrews 7:4). Under the law it is fixed and unsentimental: concerning the tithe of the herd, or of the flock, even of whatsoever passeth under the rod, the tenth shall be holy unto the LORD (Leviticus 27:32) — the animals filed under the shepherd’s staff and every tenth one counted out, without selection. Even the Levites, who lived on the tithe, tithed it: ye shall offer up an heave offering of it for the LORD, even a tenth part of the tithe (Numbers 18:26). Then Isaiah turns the number toward judgment and hope at once. When the land is emptied, yet in it shall be a tenth, and it shall return, and shall be eaten: as a teil tree, and as an oak… so the holy seed shall be the substance thereof (Isaiah 6:13). A tenth is what God claims, and a tenth is what God spares.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines TENTH as the ordinal of ten, and as a noun, the tenth part — adding that in England the tenths were an ecclesiastical due, and noting the identity of the word with tithe.
webster_full: TENTH, a. — The ordinal of ten; the first after the ninth.
TENTH, n. — The tenth part; as, he gave a tenth of his substance.
In the older English law, the tenths were the yearly tenth part of the revenue of every ecclesiastical living, paid to the crown.
TITHE is the same word in an older form, from the Saxon teotha, tenth — a fact the English reader loses when the two words are treated as unrelated.

Webster’s ecclesiastical note is a reminder that tithes were long a civil as well as a religious institution in England, which is part of why the word carries such freight in English-speaking churches.
scriptures: Genesis 14:20
And blessed be the most high God, which hath delivered thine enemies into thy hand. And he gave him tithes of all.
Leviticus 27:32
And concerning the tithe of the herd, or of the flock, even of whatsoever passeth under the rod, the tenth shall be holy unto the LORD.
Numbers 18:26

Thus speak unto the Levites, and say unto them, When ye take of the children of Israel the tithes which I have given you from them for your inheritance, then ye shall offer up an heave offering of it for the LORD, even a tenth part of the tithe.
Hebrews 7:4
Now consider how great this man was, unto whom even the patriarch Abraham gave the tenth of the spoils.
Isaiah 6:13

But yet in it shall be a tenth, and it shall return, and shall be eaten: as a teil tree, and as an oak, whose substance is in them, when they cast their leaves: so the holy seed shall be the substance thereof.
corruption_summary: The tenth is corrupted in two directions at once: by prosperity teaching that turns it into a deposit on an expected return, and by a careless liberty that treats the New Testament’s silence about a fixed percentage as permission to give nothing in particular.
corruption_paragraphs: The prosperity handling of Malachi 3:10 detaches prove me now herewith from a covenant nation under a covenant curse and turns it into a formula for personal return: sow a tenth, reap a hundredfold. The passage is addressed to a people robbing God in a specific ordinance under a specific administration, and the promised blessing is agricultural and national. To make it an investment instrument is to make God a debtor to the giver, which reverses the entire logic of Romans 4:4 — where what is earned is reckoned of debt and not of grace. Giving that expects a yield is not giving; it is a transaction, and the New Testament’s standard is elsewhere: God loveth a cheerful giver, and the Macedonians gave beyond their power out of deep poverty.

The opposite abuse trades on the fact that no fixed percentage is commanded to the church, and quietly concludes that generosity may therefore remain a feeling. But Leviticus 27:32 has the herd passing under the rod with every tenth counted out, unselected and undiscussed, and the whole shape of the law is that giving is decided in advance and by measure rather than in the moment and by mood. Paul keeps that structure exactly when he tells Corinth, upon the first day of the week let every one of you lay by him in store, as God hath prospered him. Proportion, regularity, and forethought are all carried over; only the fixed fraction is not commanded. A Christian who gives less thought to his giving than an Israelite gave to his flock has not advanced beyond the law; he has simply stopped counting.
roots_summary: Hebrew asiri (H6224), tenth, and maaser (H4643), a tithe, from eser (H6235), ten; Greek dekate (G1181), a tenth part.
roots_lines: Hebrew eser (H6235) — ten; the base of the whole family of words.
Hebrew asiri (H6224) — tenth; the tenth shall be holy unto the LORD (Leviticus 27:32).
Hebrew maaser (H4643) — a tithe, a tenth part; the standing term for the offering (Numbers 18:26; Malachi 3:10).
Greek dekate (G1181) — a tenth part, a tithe; Hebrews 7:2, 7:4, 7:8, 7:9.
Greek apodekatoo (G586) — to tithe, to pay a tenth; ye pay tithe of mint and anise and cummin (Matthew 23:23).
usage: The tenth shall be holy unto the LORD (Leviticus 27:32) — counted under the rod, not selected.
Even a tenth part of the tithe (Numbers 18:26) — those who lived on the tithe tithed it.
Yet in it shall be a tenth… so the holy seed shall be the substance thereof (Isaiah 6:13) — the remnant God keeps.
